articles.title: 'Shah Rukh Khan Sir felt that the voice suited him': Abhay Jodhpurkar recalls how Ajay-Atul, Aanand L. Rai and Irshad Kamil 'took a stand' for him for ‘Mere Naam Tu’ song from 'Zero' amid pressure to replace him with an established singer
articles.summary: Singer Abhay Jodhpurkar’s National Award win for ‘Navasachi Gauri Mazi’ from ‘Gharat Ganpati’ marks a significant milestone in a career shaped by
articles.body: Singer Abhay Jodhpurkar’s National Award win for ‘Navasachi Gauri Mazi’ from ‘Gharat Ganpati’ marks a significant milestone in a career shaped by persistence, self-doubt and the challenges of breaking into the Hindi film music industry. In an interview with Variety India, the singer opened up about how his journey to lending his voice to Shah Rukh Khan in ‘Mere Naam Tu’ from ‘Zero’ was far from straightforward. He recalled how several of his recordings were replaced by established singers, how A.R. Rahman repeatedly tried to give him opportunities, and how composers Ajay-Atul stood their ground when his voice came under scrutiny.Abhay Jodhpurkar says A.R. Rahman tried to launch him in several projectsAbhay Jodhpurkar’s association with A.R. Rahman began with ‘Godfather’ in 2012. However, despite the composer’s efforts to introduce him to larger projects, several opportunities did not translate into songs that eventually made it to the screen.“Right after being launched by A.R. Rahman Sir with ‘Godfather’ in 2012, he has been trying to launch me in a lot of projects,” Jodhpurkar told Variety India.He recalled that his recordings for several films were eventually replaced by more established voices. “From ‘Jab Tak Hai Jaan’ to ‘Kochadaiiyaan’ to a lot of films that I had done a few scratches for, ended up with me being replaced by Arijit Singh or Sonu ji or other big names,” he said.Although he had already sung more than 100 songs in the South Indian film industry, establishing himself in Hindi cinema proved difficult.“I was still a beginner down south and had done over 100 songs... Sir tried to launch me, but then, it somehow was not working out,” he recalled.The repeated setbacks began affecting his confidence. “It has somehow never worked out. And I was also losing my morale. I was like, maybe it's something in me that I need to work on or I was having self-doubt,” he said.How Abhay Jodhpurkar became Shah Rukh Khan’s voice in ‘Mere Naam Tu’A turning point came after Jodhpurkar moved to Bombay and met composer duo Ajay-Atul. They were familiar with his work, including ‘Moongil Thottam’ and his cover of ‘Jeev Rangla’ from ‘Jogwa’, and invited him to record some of their material. One of those recordings became ‘Mere Naam Tu’, the romantic track from Shah Rukh Khan’s 2018 film ‘Zero’.“What was supposed to be just a trial, just a prep” eventually turned into a defining opportunity for the singer. The song was shot over 14 days, and the team was happy with how his voice complemented the actor.“Because after the recording, the song went on to be shot for 14 days and Shah Rukh Khan sir felt that the voice suited him. Aanand L. Rai Sir, Irshad Kamil Sir, were all very happy with it,” Jodhpurkar said.However, the positive response from the creative team did not immediately eliminate concerns about having a relatively unfamiliar singer front a major Hindi film song.‘There’s a huge risk’: Singer recalls pressure to replace him on ‘Mere Naam Tu’Jodhpurkar explained that ‘Mere Naam Tu’ was one of the biggest songs in ‘Zero’, making his selection a commercial risk in the eyes of some industry stakeholders. As an unfamiliar name in Hindi cinema, he faced the possibility of being replaced by a singer with an established audience.“It was the biggest song of the film. And you're betting it with a singer who is completely unknown to the Hindi industry,” he said. “So of course, there's a huge risk. And there's a lot of debate around that and pressure from the labels to ‘let's have a big singer sing it.’”This time, however, the people backing the song refused to give in to that pressure.“They stood up and they were like, ‘No, everyone has liked it and we won't let it be replaced because he’s done a good job and we feel like it should be retained,’” he recalled.Jodhpurkar believes that decision changed the course of his career. “Had they not taken that stand for me, I would have probably not been here now,” he said, adding, “It takes a lot of guts to do that.”Abhay Jodhpurkar criticises industry gatekeeping and commercial decision-makingHis experience with ‘Mere Naam Tu’ has shaped his views on the larger Hindi film music industry. Jodhpurkar believes that even when composers support a singer, commercial considerations can lead decision-makers to favour voices that are already popular.He cited his experience with Pritam, who, according to the singer, had recommended him for several projects.“Pritam Da has pitched me to so many projects and he has insisted that we should really clean up his version but somehow they feel like ‘this won't work, we need more energy, we need accents, we need a sick voice’... popular voices,” he said.For Jodhpurkar, the underlying problem is the lack of creative authority afforded to composers and artists when commercial decisions are made by producers and other stakeholders.“People who lack creativity or who don't understand musicality are taking calls for the thing because they are the producers,” he said. “So I think that is the biggest challenge when the composer or the artist are not respected for their talent and are just treated like slaves just because they are being employed by them.”Abhay Jodhpurkar’s National Award win for ‘Navasachi Gauri Mazi’Abhay Jodhpurkar clinched the Best Male Playback Singer honor at the 72nd National Film Awards for his soulful rendition of the song "Navasachi Gauri Mazi" from the Marathi family drama film 'Gharat Ganpati'.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: Giant Moon artwork to light up Jersey church
articles.summary: Luke Jerram's Museum of the Moon will be on display free of charge at St Helier Methodist Centre.
articles.body:
A huge illuminated Moon artwork that has been displayed around the world is set to arrive in Jersey later this year.

ArtHouse Jersey has announced it will bring artist Luke Jerram's Museum of the Moon to St Helier Methodist Centre from 15 to 29 November as part of the Butterfield Public Art Series.

The 20ft (6m) installation, which features detailed Nasa imagery of the lunar surface alongside a specially created soundscape, will hang inside the church and be free for the public to visit.

The artwork has toured internationally, appearing at venues including London's Natural History Museum, Glastonbury Festival and the Commonwealth Games in Australia.

Its arrival follows the success of Jerram's Floating Earth, which attracted more than 31,000 visitors during its time in Jersey.

ArtHouse Jersey chief executive Tom Dingle said the organisation was excited to bring another of the artist's large-scale installations to the island.

"Following the incredible response to Floating Earth, we're looking forward to bringing another of Luke Jerram's extraordinary artworks to Jersey," he said.

He said the projects had a "wonderful ability to capture people's imaginations and bring the whole Island together".

Butterfield Jersey branch manager Michelle Le Blond said the organisation was proud to continue supporting public art projects that could be enjoyed by the whole community.

"Moon is an opportunity to bring people together through a shared cultural experience," she said.

The Rev Keith Sandow, superintendent of the Methodist Church in Jersey, said the church was delighted to host the installation and welcome people through its doors.

The installation will be open daily throughout its two-week stay, with dedicated quiet hours on selected dates for visitors looking for a calmer experience.

articles.title: Bristol Photo Festival to host tribute to influential photographer
articles.summary: A temporary free public gallery is set to host a tribute to the late Martin Parr as part of a photography festival.
articles.body:
A temporary free public gallery is set to host a tribute to one of Britain's most influential photographers, as part of a city-wide photography festival.

Common Sense, a tribute to late photographer Martin Parr, will be among several exhibitions at Bristol Photo Festival to be held in a hub at the Welcome Building in Bristol's business district.

Festival organisers say the idea is a way of bringing business and creative communities together.

Parr, whose colourful images captured British life, died at the age of 73 at home in Bristol in December. The gallery will be open from 15 to 18 October from 12:00 to 18:00 GMT and will host five exhibitions.

Common Sense features inexpensive colour photocopies of Parr's work to challenge conventional ideas on how photography should be exhibited.

Alongside the exhibitions, visitors will be able to take part in guided tours and a three-day masterclass with internationally renowned photographer Olivia Arthur.

The Welcome Building will also host the festival's opening event on 14 October from 18:00 to 21:00 GMT.

The wider festival will see ticketed exhibitions at Arnolfini, Bristol Museum & Art Gallery, Bristol Cathedral, IC Visual Lab, Centrespace Gallery, and Redcliffe Caves.

Festival director Alejandro Acín said the event was a "testament to the power of collaboration" at a time when "cultural organisations across the UK face significant challenges".

Acín said this year's event was made possible "through the commitment of artists, funders, partners and communities" who believed in the festival.

"At a time when cultural organisations across the UK face significant challenges, this edition is also a testament to the power of collaboration," he said.

Bristol Photo Festival 2026 will take place from 14 October to 15 November.

articles.title: 2027 Oscars power rankings: These are the top 10 best picture contenders right now
articles.summary: With the fall festivals in the books, awards columnist Glenn Whipp surveys the landscape and offers his first bold prediction of the 10 best picture nominees...
articles.body:
Venice , Telluride and Toronto have wrapped, and the New York Film Festival is winding down. Ovations have been meticulously timed. Existential crises have been parsed , not including the trauma induced by Tom Cruise's "Digger," which prudently skipped the festivals to delay, if only for a couple of weeks, the poisonous word of mouth from seeping out. ( It's still well worth seeing. )

And there have been, of course, prizes, including a Netflix movie, the Spanish maximalist melodrama "La Bola Negra," winning Toronto's People's Choice Award. That's a first for the streamer, which means we will again be asking the question: Can a Netflix film finally win the best picture Oscar?

If you've seen "The Odyssey," you probably know the answer to that question. But with more than five months (!) until the 99th Academy Awards, it's a bit early for ironclad guarantees, even if it feels like it would take the winds of Poseidon to blow "The Odyssey's" best picture campaign off course.

But it's not too soon to roll out a first set of Oscar power rankings for best picture. With apologies to "Obsession," "Fjord," "Possible Love," "You Can See Everything," "Elsinore," and whatever other movies you love (or look forward to loving), let's start counting.

Because of ongoing health issues, Mike Leigh has said that this warm and wrenching drama will be his last movie. If so, it'd be quite the capper to a career that has netted him seven Oscar nominations, five for his screenplays and two for direction. Yes, only one of his movies, "Secrets & Lies," has been nominated for best picture. But "Tender Loving Care," centered on two social service workers navigating the fraying social safety net and, in one case, anxiety about aging parents, possesses a bracing humanity full of compassion and urgency. It's also quite funny. And it boasts a great cast, including newly minted Emmy winner Kate O'Flynn, as charming here as she is on "Widow's Bay." Leigh has more than earned a final curtain call with this one.

Jordan Firstman's sincere, funny and genuinely moving debut feature has him playing a queer New York underground party promoter blindsided by the arrival of the 10-year-old son previously unknown to him. You could take issue with the uncomplicated perfection of the child, who has exquisite taste in music (Cocteau Twins, really?) and barely a trace of trauma despite the harrowing event that landed him in New York. But "Club Kid" is so assured and heartwarming that you can't muster the energy to object. There's probably going to be one feel-good movie nominated, and if it's between this and "I Play Rocky," I'll cast my lot with the one that doesn't rely so heavily on re-creating the familiar.

This 196-minute movie unfolds at, let's just say, a leisurely pace, and includes a near-20-minute scene in which a character lays out the flaws of late-stage capitalism using a whiteboard. And it's riveting. Or at least engaging. It's certainly audacious, this drama about a hardworking director of a Parisian nursing home and the way a chance friendship changes her life. The Oscars' best picture field now routinely includes two international movies, and Ryûsuke Hamaguchi's dreamlike meditation on mortality and human connection feels like a sure bet to make the cut. Virginie Efira and Tao Okamoto shared the best actress prize at Cannes and merit attention from Oscar voters as well.

Spoiler alert: One awards-season shoo-in is Julianne Moore winning every lead actress prize for her bravura work in this delightful Jesse Eisenberg comedy. Moore plays Mona, a meek, thoroughly unseen wife and mother who impulsively decides to audition for a community theater musical despite having no experience. The movie earned a huge response at its Telluride premiere , though there were some quibbles about the surprising, surreal turns the story takes. C'mon. Isn't that precisely what we want from a film? With Moore, co-star Paul Giamatti, Eisenberg's screenplay and original song (Eisenberg wrote several numbers for the film's fictional musical) assured spots, a best picture nod feels undeniable.

Olivia Wilde's dinner-party dramedy boasts a killer quartet — Wilde and Seth Rogen as longtime marrieds nursing resentments, Penélope Cruz and Edward Norton playing their upstairs neighbors — and expert direction from Wilde, who navigates the movie's tonal shifts with authority. It's wickedly funny and unsentimental and pulls off a bittersweet ending that's ambiguous enough to keep you talking long after the film ends. One of the year's most satisfying pleasures.

Speaking of endings, how many did "Project Hail Mary" have? Two? Three? I lost count. And it doesn't matter. This was the upbeat end-of-the-world movie that audiences needed at a time when the possibility of human extinction feels uncomfortably real. In a year full of Spielberg knockoffs (and an uneven movie from the man himself), this will be the one left standing.

Martin McDonagh's melancholy irreverence plays well with Oscar voters. His last two movies, "Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri" and "The Banshees of Inisherin," earned best picture nominations and a combined 16 nods. "Wild Horse Nine," a biting buddy dramedy about two mismatched CIA assassins (John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell), should continue the filmmaker's success and may even catapult Malkovich to a long-overdue Oscar. At the very least, it gave him his best role in decades.

The filmmakers, Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, are talented and charismatic, former romantic partners who still work together because that's how Europeans roll. Los Javis (they even have a fun nickname) won the directing prize at Cannes, the first of several festivals that their movie conquered, culminating in that audience award at Toronto. With its three interconnected stories that follow queer men through nearly a century of Spanish history, "La Bola Negra" has an epic feel and emotional payoff that could carry it far. Netflix is all in, opening it in select theaters Oct. 16 and giving it an exclusive 46-day theatrical window, the longest it has afforded any movie. We'll see if that puts it into the cultural conversation in a way that has eluded other Netflix contenders.

Can Denis Villeneuve's third and final "Dune" movie, which hasn't screened widely for press, take the "Lord of the Rings" trilogy path to a best picture victory? If there's resistance to giving Christopher Nolan back-to-back best picture winners, the greatest threat might come from a movie occupying the same lane, an auteur-driven epic lauded by critics and embraced by audiences. The second (and superior) "Dune" won just two Oscars, compared to the six taken by 2021's "Dune: Part One." Perhaps voters were playing the long game.

Maybe you saw it when it opened in July, contributing to its $1.75-billion box office. Maybe you're still trying to see it in Imax 70 mm, the way God (i.e., Christopher Nolan) intended. Maybe you agree with translator Emily Wilson, who thinks Nolan's movie "lacks psychological, emotional, political and ethical depth" and that its writing is "abysmal." Whichever side you're on, "The Odyssey" is probably going to sweep through the Oscars, owing to its craft and thrilling showmanship, its stellar acting and that moment when Odysseus' dog recognizes his long-absent master and wags his tail before heading off to Elysian Fields.

articles.title: Sarah Ferguson rejects tell-all speculation as expert says discretion is ‘only hope’ for future with family
articles.summary: Royal experts weigh in on Sarah Ferguson's denied memoir rumors, warning a tell-all could risk her relationship with daughters and grandchildren.
articles.body: Sarah Ferguson is setting the record straight about her intent to write a memoir. In a statement to People, representatives for the former Duchess of York shut down claims she is gearing up to release a tell-all, telling the outlet there have been "no discussions" about a book deal. "She is not writing a personal memoir," they said. Rumors she was preparing to release a memoir started in late September, when The Sun reported Ferguson was "days away" from signing a lucrative book deal which would cover her ex-husband, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's relationship with Jeffrey Epstein. FORMER PRINCE ANDREW, SARAH FERGUSON DUBBED ROYAL FAMILY’S ‘BONNIE AND CLYDE’ AS EPSTEIN FALLOUT GROWS: AUTHOR "The other day it was announced by the Sun newspaper that Sarah Ferguson was attempting to write a book, an all-tell book, giving all the secrets away about the royal family. It was strongly denied very quickly by her PR team," royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital. articles.title: ‘Other Mommy’ tops the box office with $27.5M; ‘The Social Reckoning’ opens to $5.5M
articles.summary: The Jessica Chastain horror “Other Mommy” topped the North American box office this weekend with a bigger audience than expected, while “The Social Reckoning” got off to a lackluster start.
articles.body: The Jessica Chastain horror “Other Mommy” topped the North American box office this weekend with a bigger audience than expected, while “The Social Reckoning” got off to a lackluster start. ‘Other Mommy’ is another win for horror “Other Mommy,” released by Universal Pictures, earned $27.5 million in its first few days in 3,365 theaters, according to studio estimates on Sunday. The movie, about a sinister supernatural creature that terrorizes a young girl who thinks it’s her mother, got dismal reviews from both critics and audiences. It also joins the ranks of “Megalopolis” and “Hereditary” with a D+ CinemaScore. But with a production budget of around $19 million, it’s also another win for the horror genre and producer Blumhouse Atomic Monster, which was behind “Backrooms” and “Obsession.” “Other Mommy” opened in 50 international markets as well, boosting its global debut to $45.2 million. Jim Orr, Universal’s head of domestic distribution, noted that the audience gender divide was evenly split and about 2/3 were between 18 and 34 years old. “No matter how you look at it, everybody turned out for it. It wasn’t just one particular demographic,” Orr said. “That usually is a very good sign.” ‘The Social Reckoning’ fails to connect “The Social Reckoning,” the weekend’s other big release, was not as lucky, earning an estimated $5.5 million from 2,606 North American theaters. Aaron Sorkin wrote and directed the film about a Facebook whistleblower who leaked incriminating documents to a Wall Street Journal reporter. Sixteen years ago, “The Social Network,” which Sorkin wrote and David Fincher directed, opened to over $22 million and went on to gross over $224 million worldwide, receiving eight Oscar nominations and winning three. A similar fate might be a stretch for “The Social Reckoning,” which stars Mikey Madison, Jeremy Allen White and Jeremy Strong and received mixed-to-negative reviews from critics. Audiences gave it a B- CinemaScore. According to reports, the Sony Pictures release cost around $30 million to produce, not accounting for marketing and promotion. Paul Dergarabedian, Rentrak’s head of marketplace trends, said October is a time when studios take chances and it doesn’t always work out. “These movies that are topical in nature, sometimes they resonate with the culture, sometimes they don’t,” said Dergarabedian. “You don’t always know what’s going to connect with audiences.” He compared “The Social Reckoning” to “Digger,” which fell 60% in its second weekend. The overall box office is still up “The Social Reckoning” opened behind several holdovers as well. The Anne Hathaway psychological thriller “Verity” took second place with $11.5 million, down 64% from its opening weekend. In third place, “Resident Evil” added $8.4 million, bringing its domestic total to $138.5 million. The Brad Pitt survival thriller “Heart of the Beast” took fourth with $7.1 million. Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey ” also made an encore appearance in the top 10 in its 13th weekend in theaters where it was back in 12 IMAX 70 mm locations. It added $2 million from 560 North American theaters, bringing its domestic total just shy of $623 million. Several high-profile films opened in limited release this weekend as well. The Cannes Palme d’Or winner “Fjord” debuted on four screens this weekend where it made $124,000. Alex Gibney’s Elon Musk documentary “Musk,” which runs nearly four hours, made $68,900 from four locations. And Chris Rock’s “Misty Green” made $85,716 from six locations through Sunday. The annual domestic box office crossed the $8 billion mark on Friday and is up over 19% from last year. According to Rentrak, that’s about 8% behind 2019. Top 10 movies by domestic box office With final domestic figures being released Monday, this list factors in the estimated ticket sales for Friday through Sunday at U.S. and Canadian theaters, according to Rentrak: 1. “Other Mommy,” $27.5 million. 2. “Verity,” $11.5 million. 3. “Resident Evil,” $8.4 million. 4. “Heart of the Beast,” $7.1 million. 5. “The Social Reckoning,” $5.5 million. 6. “Forgotten Island,” $4.5 million. 7. “Primetime,” $4 million. 8. “Digger,” $3.2 million. 9. “Angel and the Badman,” $2.1 million. 10. “The Odyssey,” $2 million.

articles.title: Kate Gosselin's son discusses mom's alleged abuse ahead of new memoir
articles.summary: Collin Gosselin's memoir "In the Shadow of Eight" is out on Oct. 13.
articles.body:
Former "Jon & Kate Plus 8" star Collin Gosselin is speaking out about alleged abuse he says he endured growing up.

Ahead of his new memoir, "In the Shadow of Eight," out Oct. 13, Gosselin sat down with ABC News' Juju Chang and detailed what he alleged happened behind the scenes of the popular reality show when the cameras stopped rolling.

"Simply put, my whole life that I lived was a lie," Gosselin said. "All the things you see on TV, lies."

Gosselin, one of six kids born to reality TV stars Jon Gosselin and Kate Gosselin , rose to fame as a child on TLC's "Jon & Kate Plus 8," which documented the family raising their twins, Madelyn and Cara , and sextuplets Leah, Hannah, Alexis, Joel, Aaden and Collin.

Jon Gosselin and Kate Gosselin announced their divorce in 2009 at the end of an episode of their show, which aired in June that year.

After the divorce, Kate Gosselin was granted primary custody of all eight children, and the family's reality series was later renamed "Kate Plus 8," focusing on Kate Gosselin's life as a divorced mother raising the twins and sextuplets.

Collin Gosselin claimed it was after his parents' divorce that his mother allegedly isolated him from his father and made him sleep in a locked room in their basement. He alleged that the abuse got so bad that it caught the attention of one of his teachers, who noticed his swollen earlobe, which he said happened after his mother allegedly "dragged" him across the room by his earlobe.

"My teacher saw ... and then I talked to my guidance counselor, and I told them about it," he said, speaking with Chang. "And my mom was not very happy that I spoke about that."

Collin Gosselin said he was eventually pulled out of school by his mom when he was in the fourth grade and recalled being "too afraid to say anything" when child protective services entered the picture.

When he tried to run away, Collin Gosselin alleges his mom zip-tied his hands and feet together and locked him in a basement room.

Collin Gosselin said his mother had him removed from the home days before his 12th birthday and placed him in an institution where he was given medication and had almost no contact with his family.

"I was told, 'This is for your own good,'" he said. "I threatened my mom's income, I threatened her image, and people will do anything to protect their reputation, especially my mom."

In 2016, Kate Gosselin spoke to ABC News about Collin Gosselin, claiming he was sent to get treatment for educational and social challenges. At the time, she said her decision was "the best thing I can do for him right now."

When asked at the time about reports from staffers about abuse that Collin Gosselin claimed he endured from his mom, Kate Gosselin called the reports "unfounded."

"I'm in the public eye," she said in the 2016 interview. "I have been investigated many times…. It's always unfounded, obviously."

After a year in the institution, Collin Gosselin said he wrote a crayon-scratched note to his dad and had a friend sneak it out to him.

The note read, "I'm counting on you to get me out of here. Daddy, I love you. Save me."

Collin Gosselin said that two years after being sent to the institution -- after his dad went through the court system to get him released -- he moved in with his dad and his sister Hannah, who had decided to leave Kate Gosselin's care.

In his book, Collin Gosselin writes that in 2023, after years of his mother claiming he suffered from various mental and behavioral challenges, he underwent an independent psychological evaluation, which did not reveal any mental health diagnoses at that time.

He told Chang the results didn't surprise him.

"I knew I'd go through life every day as a functioning member of society. It's just that I needed it on paper," he said.

ABC News reached out to the doctor who Collin Gosselin says conducted the evaluation, but they declined to comment on the matter.

Today, Collin Gosselin is in college and is studying finance. When asked by Chang if he would be open to reconnecting with his six other siblings -- Maddie, Cara, Alexis, Aaden, Leah and Joel -- he said he "would love to" but understands that his relationship with them will never be the same.

In a message to his siblings, he said, "No matter what's happened or what was said, no matter how things look from the outside, I love you, I always have and always will."

ABC News reached out to Kate Gosselin and TLC for comment but did not receive a response. Jon Gosselin declined ABC News' request for an interview for this story.

articles.title: Alba Carrillo, sobre 'La bola negra': "Los Javis han calmado los llantos de los miles de fusilados"
articles.standfirst: La colaboradora televisiva comparte en Instagram una reflexión sobre la película de Javier Calvo y Javier Ambrossi, la memoria histórica y el legado de Federico García Lorca
articles.summary: La colaboradora televisiva comparte en Instagram una reflexión sobre la película de Javier Calvo y Javier Ambrossi, la memoria histórica y el legado de Federico García Lorca
articles.body: Alba Carrillo ha compartido en sus redes sociales una extensa reflexión sobre 'La bola negra', la película dirigida por Javier Calvo y Javier Ambrossi, conocidos como Los Javis. La colaboradora televisiva ha explicado que la cinta le ha hecho pensar en la memoria histórica, el dolor de las familias de las víctimas de la represión y la importancia de recuperar historias que, durante décadas, han permanecido silenciadas. "Había estado mala y hasta hoy no había podido ir. Reconozco que también me daba miedo (no estoy para bajar mis defensas)", comienza el texto que ha publicado en Instagram. Carrillo reconoce así que tenía ciertas reservas antes de ver la película, aunque su valoración posterior es rotunda: "Los Javis con esta película se han puesto a excavar hasta dejarse las uñas. Esto se llama REPARACIÓN con mayúsculas". La reflexión de la colaboradora va más allá de una recomendación cinematográfica. En su publicación, vincula el relato de la película con la memoria de quienes sufrieron la represión y con la necesidad de recuperar el recuerdo de las personas que fueron asesinadas y cuyos restos todavía no han sido localizados. Uno de los pasajes centrales de su mensaje se refiere a Federico García Lorca y a la búsqueda de sus restos. Carrillo recupera unas palabras atribuidas al músico y poeta Leonard Cohen sobre la necesidad de encontrar el cuerpo del escritor granadino: "No entiendo cómo España no ha excavado con sus manos todo el campo de Granada para recuperar el cuerpo de su poeta". A partir de esa referencia, la colaboradora expresa su incomprensión ante el hecho de que todavía haya familias que no hayan podido recuperar los restos de sus seres queridos. "Somos herederos del nulo reconocimiento del dolor de miles de familias que tienen aún a sus seres queridos en cunetas. Somos los portadores de la no reparación", escribe. Carrillo considera que la película de Los Javis contribuye a mantener viva esa memoria y a acercar al público historias que, a su juicio, no deberían caer en el olvido. En su opinión, el valor de la obra reside también en su capacidad para generar una reflexión colectiva sobre el pasado y sus consecuencias en el presente. "Es la primera vez que veo salir de un cine a la gente en silencio, en una suerte de duelo colectivo", asegura sobre su experiencia tras la proyección. Una reacción que interpreta como una muestra del impacto emocional que le ha provocado la cinta. La colaboradora también dedica parte de su publicación a destacar la dimensión artística de la película. Para ella, 'La bola negra' trasciende el relato cinematográfico y conecta con la poesía y el legado de Lorca. "Es una obra maestra porque solo desde la cultura y el arte, como nos enseñó Federico, se puede dar el consuelo que no nos da la vida", afirma. Carrillo llega a comparar el nivel poético de la película con el del propio escritor granadino y sostiene que Los Javis han logrado trasladar esa sensibilidad a su trabajo. La reflexión termina con una referencia a una frase que, según explica, le ha recordado a una de sus películas favoritas, 'El tigre y la nieve', de Roberto Benigni. "¿Sois de los que creéis que puede nevar en verano o sois de los que portáis el fusil?", plantea. La publicación de Alba Carrillo se suma a las reacciones de espectadores que han compartido sus impresiones sobre una película que aborda tanto las historias personales de sus protagonistas como la huella que dejan la represión y el silencio en la memoria colectiva.

articles.body: Ben Affleck's son Samuel appears to have developed a taste for Lamborghinis, four years after he accidentally backed one into another luxury car. BEN AFFLECK ADMITS HIS TEENAGER ROASTED HIS DATING HISTORY WHILE AT DINNER "I see my son now, you know, and he's a lot like me," Affleck said. "My son's like, ‘Dad, you should get a Lambo,’" the Oscar winner recalled with a laugh. "'What? A Lambo? Are you f---ing crazy? At the time, Affleck allowed Samuel, then 10, to sit in the driver's seat of a bright yellow Lamborghini SUV before the boy accidentally put the car into reverse and backed into a white BMW. Samuel was photographed jumping out of the Lamborghini to inspect the vehicles, while Affleck also checked for damage. The "Gone Girl" star was later photographed hugging Samuel while talking with Lopez, whom he married in July 2022. The former couple finalized their divorce in January 2025. At the time, representatives for Affleck and 777 Exotics both told the New York Post there was no damage to either vehicle. An employee at the rental dealership also said there were no hard feelings following the fender-bender. KRISTIN CAVALLARI ADMITS HER KIDS FLY COACH WHILE SHE SITS IN FIRST CLASS "Affleck loves cars," the dealership employee told the New York Post. "We hope they come in again." The Lamborghini isn't the first high-priced item to catch Samuel's eye. MARK WAHLBERG ADMITS HOLLYWOOD FAME COMES WITH ‘BAGGAGE’ FOR HIS KIDS In the clip, Affleck and Samuel browsed sneakers at a convention, where Samuel spotted the Dior shoes. articles.title: Kelly Clarkson's beef with a Brooklyn store has gone viral. Neither side is backing down.
articles.summary: Clarkson claims that the item she wanted to purchase had a $15,000 price tag, but the Brooklyn store insists it was never for sale. The back-and-forth's sinc...
articles.body:
Kelly Clarkson is feuding with an independent shop in Brooklyn, N.Y., after accusing an employee of giving her the Pretty Woman treatment and refusing to sell her an expensive singing bird, which the store maintains wasn't for sale.

Clarkson wrote on X Saturday that she drove to Brooklyn Heights to visit the shop, Art of Play, intending to buy "a few things." But during her visit she says she was "looked at as if I couldn't afford it" and was told by an employee they could find "something comparable" for her to purchase.

"Y'all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts character in Pretty Woman," she added, referencing a memorable scene in the 1990 romantic comedy in which Roberts's character, Vivian, is snubbed by saleswomen at an upscale clothing boutique because of her appearance.

Responding to Clarkson's accusation, the store posted on Instagram o n Sunday , saying that the item she asked about was a "one-of-a-kind singing and dancing bird" named Molly, which is used in its magic shows. The store said the fixture was "permanently attached to the wall and isn't for sale."

Art of Play, which specializes in unusual games, puzzles, curiosities and also hosts magic shows in a hidden theater, said it was "surreal" to be the focus of "such widespread outrage after just one mention by a celebrity."

"Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by 8 million people who have never visited our store," the shop said.

Clarkson disputed the store's explanation, sharing an image that she said showed a $15,000 price tag on the bird."Okay, cool. So you're not only rude, you're also a liar. Got it," she wrote on X .

In a follow-up statement on Instagram , the shop offered further details, saying it had explained to Clarkson that a "nearly identical automaton" could be purchased directly from the artist for $15,000.

"We explained all of this to Kelly Clarkson," the store said. "We also offered to show her a different singing bird automaton, made by a traditional clockmaking shop in Germany, that she could have taken home with her that day. It costs about $2,000. She did not stick around long enough to see it."The dispute has divided social media users, with some accusing the shop of lying about whether the mechanical bird was for sale.

Food podcast host Joey Camasta commented on the store's Instagram post: "I was literally there in August and saw Molly, there was a price tag on it. It most definitely was for sale."

One commenter criticized the store's response : "Their 'apology' was not only dishonest, it was so patronising and passive-aggressive that it gave us all a taste of what you experienced, and further proved your point. Rancid."

Another X user, Nigel Carreiro , wrote: "since u been gone the $15,000 price tag has also mysteriously disappeared."

Others questioned Clarkson's take, accusing her of doubling down on naming and shaming an independent business.

"It seems as though someone tried to purchase a thing that was not for sale, they were re-directed to an alternative...and then stormed out and made a negative social media post about a small business," another commenter wrote .

Others pointed to a social media post from Art of Play from a month earlier outlining that the bird wasn't for sale.

Yahoo has reached out to both parties for comment.

Clarkson moved from Los Angeles to New York City in 2023, relocating The Kelly Clarkson Show there. She announced in February that the show would end after seven seasons, with its final episode airing in August, the same month her Las Vegas residency concluded. Clarkson is currently appearing as a coach on Season 30 of The Voice .

Clarkson's dispute follows a number of high-profile clashes between celebrities and businesses. In 2016, Zendaya accused a grocery store employee of treating her unfairly while she was trying to purchase gift cards, saying she believed the encounter was racially motivated. In 2005, Oprah Winfrey criticized luxury retailer Hermès , alleging she was turned away from its Paris store 15 minutes after closing time, despite her account that other shoppers were still inside. The CEO of Hermès USA later apologized on her show, describing the employee who turned her away as "very, very rigid."

articles.title: Quote of the day by Bear Grylls: ‘There is little faith involved in setting out on a journey where the destination is certain…when we do not know the route ahead and cannot be certain we will ever return,' the TV star’s lesson about doing things with uncertainty and taking a chance
articles.summary: Explore Bear Grylls' insightful quote on adventure, faith, and growth in the face of uncertainty. Learn how stepping out of comfort zones leads to personal development and bravery.
articles.body: Bear Grylls is possibly one of the most resilient and adventurous people on earth and has also managed to create a career out of it. Known for shows such as ‘Running Wild with Bear Grylls,' ‘Celebrity Bear Hunt,' and ‘Man Vs Wild,' to name a few, Grylls has created his own unique identity in the entertainment industry. His quote for the day comes from his experience and the adventures he has been through in his life.The quote of the day reads, "There is little faith involved in setting out on a journey where the destination is certain and every step in between has been mapped in detail. Bravery and trust are about leaving camp in the dark, when we do not know the route ahead and cannot be certain we will ever return.”What does the quote mean?Bear Grylls wrote these words in his 2012 book, ‘A Survival Guide for Life: How to Achieve Your Goals, Thrive in Adversity, and Grow in Character.' The TV star uses his experience on expeditions to draw parallels between everyday life. The quote is inherently about understanding that a person can only move forward and face things like growth, trust, and bravery when they step into uncertainty.When every step of a path is planned, safe, and guaranteed, and you know what will happen every step of the way, there are high chances that we stay within our comfort zones and what we know best. However, true adventure, change, and growth in life only come when you encounter uncertainty in your path or you take the roads less traveled.At the end of the day it is all about understanding that sometimes staying within your comfort zone can deter your growth, whereas doing something new and different that you are not used to may end up leading you towards your destination and goal in life. Real commitment means accepting that the journey might permanently change you or that you might not be able to go back to the way things were. True bravery isn't the absence of fear or the presence of a safety net; it is deciding that the journey is worth taking despite the absence of guarantees or without a comfort zone.All about Bear Grylls’ early yearsGrylls was born Edward Michael Grylls on June 7, 1974, in Donaghadee, Northern Ireland. He grew up with a passion for outdoor survival and adventure from a young age, and his father would often encourage him to build upon his skills. His older sister, Lara, gave him the nickname "Bear" when he was just a week old, and it stuck for life, now becoming part of his multi-million-dollar brand.His father, Sir Michael Grylls, is a Conservative politician, former Royal Marine and a member of the Royal Yacht Squadron. Because of this, Bear’s father taught him how to sail, build boats, tie knots, and scale the sea cliffs along the Isle of Wight, where they had moved when he was four years old. During his school years, he was heavily bullied, which inspired him to train in Shotokan Karate to build self-defense skills and discipline. He even travelled to Japan to train in the art at the time and earned a 2nd dan black belt as a teenager, making him one of the youngest in the UK to achieve it then. He also joined the Cub Scouts, learned skydiving, and developed an interest in extreme sports and survival techniques.His love for extreme sports, survival skills, and adventure followed him from his youth into his adulthood, and the rest is history. As for his studies, Grylls studied at Eton College; however, he was never interested in traditional academics. Instead, he created the school’s very first mountaineering club, organizing climbing trips for fellow students.After he dropped out of school, he travelled around a lot, went to India and hiked across the Himalayas in Sikkim and West Bengal. At the time, he almost considered joining the Indian Army, though he ended up returning to the UK to study Spanish and German at university. He wrote about his childhood and his transition into showbiz in his books, including ‘Mud, Sweat, and Tears: The Autobiography’ and ‘A Survival Guide for Life: How to Achieve Your Goals, Thrive in Adversity, and Grow in Character.'About Bear Grylls’ careerBefore starting his career in showbiz, he served in the British Special Forces Reserves with the 21 SAS Regiment (21 Special Air Service) from 1994 to 1997. After getting injured in 1996 during a free-fall parachuting exercise over Zambia, the star embarked on several high-profile world records and extreme adventures. These included climbing Mount Everest, leading a team on the first jet-ski circumnavigation of the British Isles, and crossing the frozen North Atlantic in an open 11-meter rigid-inflatable boat, among many other feats.Other than that, he also built quite a successful TV career, which included shows like ‘Escape to the Legion,' ‘Man vs. Wild/Born Survivor,' ‘Running Wild with Bear Grylls,' ‘The Island with Bear Grylls,' and many others.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: No Man’s Sky is coming to the iPhone and iPad
articles.summary: Hello Games has announced that its sci-fi exploration game No Man’s Sky is coming to the iPhone and iPad on October 28th.
articles.body: The No Man’s Sky universe is about to get a little bit smaller — but in a good way. Hello Games announced that its long-running sci-fi exploration game will be coming to iOS, with versions for both the iPhone and iPad available starting on October 28th. According to Hello’s Sean Murray, the mobile version of the game is essentially the full No Man’s Sky experience. “I guess I should say this is not No Man’s Sky Lite,” he wrote in a blog post. It includes all of the game’s many, many updates that have come out since launch — like the gigantic Voyagers expansion from last year — and the only major features missing will be multiplayer and the planetary settlements. Murray likens the iOS version to when the game initially launched on the original Switch. “On Switch we have listened to players and built from there, including with a much expanded version on Switch 2,” he says. “Based on feedback and player numbers we will support iOS in a similar way.” The game will be playable on the iPhone 11 and 3rd generation iPad Air and above, and the studio says that the download comes in at a surprisingly scant 5GB. It also has newly-designed touch controls, as well as support for controllers, screen casting, and mouse-and-keyboard on the iPad. Murray also notes that “Perhaps most importantly we’ve put tons of work into battery life and thermodynamics, and we’re super proud that No Man’s Sky can be enjoyed for really long comfortable play sessions.” It’ll be “free to try” at launch, though it’s not clear how much the full version will cost. It’s now been a decade since No Man’s Sky first launched, and the game has changed dramatically since its debut. iOS will be joining a huge list of supported platforms, including Mac, PC, and essentially every modern console, and there’s also a VR version available. Just as significant, Hello has continued to keep the game vibrant with a constant stream of free expansions, including the recent Cosmos update in September, which fleshed out the vast expanse of space with more things to explore.

articles.title: ‘Miami Vice ’85’ First Look: Michael B. Jordan and Austin Butler Are Tubbs and Crockett
articles.summary: Michael B. Jordan and Austin Butler play Tubbs and Crocket in Top Gun: Maverick director Joseph Kosinski's Miami Vice '85.
articles.body:
Our first look at Michael B. Jordan and Austin Butler in character for "Miami Vice '85" arrived on Monday, as production is now underway on Universal's big-screen adaptation of the iconic TV series.

Joseph Kosinski, the filmmaker behind "Top Gun: Maverick" and "F1," ideated the fresh spin on the IP and directs from a screenplay by Dan Gilroy ("Nightcrawler").

Jordan plays Tubbs and Butler plays Crockett in "Miami Vice '85," with a swell ensemble cast that includes Alden Ehrenreich, Camila Morrone, Walton Goggins, Danny Ramirez, John Leguizamo, Andre Holland, Michael Irby and Whitney Peak.

Kosinski reunites with his "F1" and "Top Gun: Maverick" cinematographer, Claudio Miranda, on the project, and produces alongside Dylan Clark.

The film is, of course, based on the popular 1980s TV series "Miami Vice" starring Don Johnson and Philip Michael Thomas as detectives working undercover in Miami. The show was groundbreaking for its use of popular music and drawing from the culture at the time, much of which was owed to director Michael Mann's vision for the series.

After becoming a respected film director in his own right, Mann famously adapted the show into a feature film in 2006 with Colin Farrell and Jamie Foxx playing Crockett and Tubbs. That gritty take on the material garnered mixed reviews and an underwhelming box office, but has since earned a sort of cult fandom. In fact, Mann is releasing yet another cut of the movie on home video later this year.

Universal sees "Miami Vice '85" as a tentpole and has set the film for a May 19, 2028 release only in theaters. See the first looks below.

articles.title: In 1993, Kim Basinger was ordered to pay $8.9 million after backing out of 'Boxing Helena'; the verdict was later overturned
articles.summary: Hollywood actress Kim Basinger found herself at the centre of a major legal dispute in 1993 after withdrawing from the independent film Boxing Helena.
articles.body: Hollywood actress Kim Basinger found herself at the centre of a major legal dispute in 1993 after withdrawing from the independent film Boxing Helena. A Los Angeles jury ruled against her, ordering her to pay millions of dollars to the film’s production company, Main Line Pictures, over an alleged agreement to star in the project.The verdict drew widespread attention because it raised questions about the legal consequences of informal agreements in the film industry. However, the decision was overturned by a California appeals court in 1994 because the jury’s findings failed to clearly distinguish Basinger’s responsibility from that of her personal services company.How the dispute beganThe controversy began in the early 1990s, when Main Line Pictures approached Basinger about playing the lead character in Boxing Helena, a psychological drama written and directed by Jennifer Lynch. In December 1990, the production company sent Basinger the screenplay and subsequently offered her $500,000, along with additional compensation tied to the film’s financial performance.Basinger initially expressed interest in the project. She met Lynch in January 1991 to discuss the film and the role. However, disagreements developed over the proposed arrangement, and Main Line Pictures maintained that the actress had committed herself to the production through an agreement that she later failed to honour.By June 1991, the production company had learned that Basinger would not be appearing in the film. Main Line Pictures subsequently filed a lawsuit against the actress and her company, Mighty Wind Inc., alleging breach of contract. Basinger disputed the claim that she was personally bound by an enforceable agreement. The central issue was whether the discussions and documents exchanged between the parties amounted to a binding commitment.The $8.9 million verdict in 1993The case went to trial in Los Angeles, where Main Line Pictures argued that Basinger’s withdrawal had caused significant financial losses. The company hadrelied on her involvement when making arrangements to secure financing and sell distribution rights in overseas markets. According to the court record, foreign presales for the film with Basinger’s name attached had reached $6.8 million before her departure affected the production’s plans.In March 1993, the jury sided with the production company. It awarded $7,421,694 in damages for breach of contract and an additional $1.5 million for what it considered a bad-faith denial of the agreement, bringing the initial award to approximately $8.9 million. The jury declined to impose further punitive damages.The decision was a significant setback for Basinger, who had argued that no binding contract existed in the form alleged by the production company. The case also attracted attention across Hollywood, where negotiations between actors, agents and producers sometimes begin with verbal commitments before formal contracts are signed.The amount was subsequently reduced by the trial judge in May 1993. The court removed the additional $1.5 million award as duplicative, leaving $7,421,694 in damages, and awarded the production company approximately $713,522 in legal fees and costs. The resulting judgment totalled about $8.14 million.Why the verdict was overturnedBasinger and Mighty Wind appealed the judgment. On September 22, 1994, the California Court of Appeal reversed the ruling, finding that the jury’s verdict forms were legally ambiguous.The central problem was the wording used in the jury’s questions, which repeatedly referred to “Basinger and/or Mighty Wind.” The appellate court explained that this wording did not establish whether Basinger personally had entered into and breached a contract, whether her company was responsible, or whether both parties were liable.This distinction was important because Mighty Wind was a separate legal entity through which Basinger’s acting services were arranged. The court held that the company could not automatically be treated as identical to the actress simply because it handled her professional services. The production company had not pursued the legal argument necessary to establish that the corporation and Basinger should be treated as one entity for liability purposes.The appeals court did not rule that no agreement had existed. In fact, its decision acknowledged that there was substantial evidence supporting the possibility that both Basinger and her company had entered into an oral contract. However, the evidence did not compel that conclusion, and the jury had failed to identify which party was responsible. The court therefore overturned the judgment rather than deciding the underlying contractual dispute in Basinger’s favour.What happened after the appeal?The reversal brought an end to the original judgment, but it did not automatically resolve the dispute between Basinger and Main Line Pictures. The appeals court’s decision allowed the case to be retried, and the prospect of further proceedings remained after the ruling.The controversy had also become a major financial issue for the actress. Basinger filed for bankruptcy in 1993 following the original judgment, illustrating the potential consequences of a large damages award even before the appeals process was completed. Contemporary reporting in September 1994 noted that the verdict had been overturned while proceedings connected to her bankruptcy were still under way.The film itself eventually moved forward with actress Sherilyn Fenn in the lead role. Written and directed by Jennifer Lynch, Boxing Helena told the disturbing story of a surgeon whose obsession with a woman leads him to hold her captive after amputating her limbs. The project became widely associated with the legal controversy surrounding Basinger’s withdrawal.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: 'The Social Reckoning' Review: Zuckerberg, Facebook are the enemy in preachy slop disguised as journo drama
articles.summary: Fox News Digital reviews Sony Pictures' "The Social Reckoning" starring Jeremy Strong, Jeremy Allen White and Mikey Madison. Written and directed by Aaron Sorkin.
articles.body: In the era of Trump 2.0, the tech titans once championed by the liberal left have been ostracized for the appearance of embracing or bending the knee to President Donald Trump after the 2024 election, whether it be Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos or — in this particular case — Mark Zuckerberg. Zuckerberg, co-founder of Facebook and the CEO of Meta, was famously depicted on the big screen in the 2010 film, "The Social Network," which followed his creation of the culture-reshaping social media platform from his Harvard dorm room and the lawsuits that ensued after. Directed by David Fincher, written by Aaron Sorkin and with dead ringer Jesse Eisenberg playing Zuckerberg, the trio delivered one of this century's greatest films that truly captured the zeitgeist of the emerging digital age. Sorkin won an Oscar for Best Adapted Screenplay and both Fincher and Eisenberg scored nominations in their respective categories. But 16 years later, what's been billed as a sequel to "The Social Network" only tarnishes its legacy. DIGGER REVIEW: TOM CRUISE DESTROYS THE PLANET IN ALEJANDRO IÑÁRRITU'S GRANDIOSE, MESSY POLITICAL SATIRE For "The Social Reckoning," neither Fincher nor Eisenberg chose to return, leaving Sorkin to both write and direct the sequel that no one really asked for and cast Jeremy Strong ("Succession," "The Apprentice") as Zuckerberg. The sequel revisits the Wall Street Journal's bombshell series of reports dubbed "The Facebook Files," spearheaded by investigative reporter Jeff Horowitz (Jeremy Allen White) and Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison). The uncovered dirt ranged from Facebook implementing algorithms that drove its users to join hate groups to the company knowing about the toxicity of Instagram on the mental health of young girls. Most of us can agree that social media platforms broadly, not just Facebook, have negative impacts on society, while also having benefits. What was previously reported about Facebook has been a stain on the company. And maybe that does warrant a movie. What's disagreeable is the narrow universe Sorkin creates, one where Facebook, and only Facebook, is responsible for fomenting right-wing radicalism and that left-wing radicalism is nonexistent. ‘PRIMETIME’ REVIEW: ROBERT PATTINSON CHANNELS CHRIS HANSEN IN RIVETING DRAMATIZATION OF ‘TO CATCH A PREDATOR’ In the film, Haugen, the Facebook data scientist who made waves when she came forward in 2021, is haunted by a former friend, who she described as once being a "progressive" but has been radicalized by the platform becoming an unhinged racist. The film also blames Facebook for the spread of QAnon conspiracy theories and vaccine "lies," as well as Jan. 6. The culminating scene of "The Social Reckoning" involves Zuckerberg and his staff rushing to their war room to watch news coverage of the Capitol riot. The rioters might as well have been waving flags that read, "Brought to you by Facebook," at least according to Sorkin. Everyone around Zuckerberg demanded him to ban Trump from their platform. And as we all know, Zuckerberg acquiesced. Haugen's findings, at least presented in this film, show that Facebook makes people racists. There's no mention of any sort of far-left radicalization Americans have witnessed, (or "Woke 1" as AOC recently coined) nor any mention of the Black Lives Matter riots that erupted across the country in the months leading up to Jan. 6. Lest we forget that the COVID lockdowns truly fueled societal paranoia, there isn't any "reckoning" from Sorkin for the government officials who enforced them. For a man who prides himself on his hyper-intellectual dialogue, Sorkin finds little room for nuance. ‘RESIDENT EVIL’ REVIEW: DIRECTOR ZACH CREGGER DELIVERS INFECTIOUS REBOOT TO GORY VIDEO GAME FRANCHISE The film's only saving grace is how it goes about Zuckerberg's stance as a free speech absolutist. Sorkin broadly portrays him as a sociopathic villain who cares about the bottom line at society's expense. But there's one scene where he's arguing with a former investor (played by Bill Burr) that Facebook is a public square and that its users don't need to be treated like children, as Burr's character deems Zuckerberg's philosophy reckless for letting falsehoods go unfettered. It's clear Sorkin wants his audience to be on Team Burr in that particular scene, but true champions of free speech side with Zuckerberg — at least until he caves to pressure and bans Trump. "The Social Reckoning" attempts to be the "All the President's Men" of the social media era, but it lacks any emotional depth beyond its blatant appeal to partisan leftists. None of the film's three leads operate like normal human beings (to be fair, Zuckerberg's public persona has always been, well, peculiar). Every scene between Horowitz and Haugen is full of unnaturally witty and scholarly dialogue that could've easily been borrowed from "The West Wing." It's tiresome. 'THE DOG STARS' REVIEW: JACOB ELORDI FIGHTS FOR SURVIVAL IN RIDLEY SCOTT'S DULL POST-APOCALYPTIC WESTERN Unlike his predecessor in "The Social Network," Strong looks remotely nothing like Zuckerberg but gives a dedicated performance and, admittedly, kind of nails the voice. The Facebook chief had no involvement with either film, so it's difficult to tell where the reality ends and the fiction begins. Yet Eisenberg's Zuckerberg was far more emotionally ranging, while Strong's Zuckerberg is essentially an alien-like caricature. There's also a stark contrast in the pure filmmaking. Without Fincher at the helm, Sorkin is left artistically rudderless despite his top-notch collaborators like Oscar-nominated cinematographer Jeff Cronenweth (who previously shot "The Social Network") and Oscar-winning composer Alexandre Desplat. This isn't Sorkin's first time in the director's chair. There's no questioning his talents as a screenwriter, but while he has successfully found his unique voice on the page, he has yet to craft his own vision as a director. Having rewatched "The Social Network," it's wild to think both were written by Sorkin. One is captivating, smooth, biting and tangible to the average viewer. The other is dull, disjointed, self-righteous and elitist. CLICK HERE FOR THE LATEST MEDIA AND CULTURE NEWS The Verdict "The Social Reckoning" tries to recreate the magic of its predecessor. In reality, it's leftist revisionist slop disguised as a harrowing journalist drama. It's a film that only caters to a narrow audience of coastal liberals who despise Zuckerberg/Trump and journalists who regard themselves as heroes — many happen to be both. What's unfortunate is that "The Social Reckoning" doesn't exist with the purpose of entertaining. Its purpose is to lecture. And for that reason, Sorkin ought to log off. ★ — SKIP IT "The Social Reckoning" is rated R for language. Running time: 1 hour, 52 minutes. In theaters now. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

articles.title: Zaniolo opens up about ‘turbulent summer’ and Alaba’s Udinese move
articles.summary: Italy international Nicolò Zaniolo insists he ‘always wanted’ to stay at Udinese and is delighted to welcome David Alaba: ‘It demonstrates the strength and a...
articles.body:
Italy international Nicolò Zaniolo insists he 'always wanted' to stay at Udinese and is delighted to welcome David Alaba: 'It demonstrates the strength and ambition of the club.'

Former Real Madrid and Bayern Munich star Alaba joined Udinese on a free transfer during the international break and is expected to make his debut tonight against Torino.

Italy international Zaniolo spoke about Alaba's first days at the club: "Udinese are undoubtedly a historic Italian club that, by its very nature, have always had great players and plenty of talent," the striker told Calciomercato.com.

INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA – JULY 02: David Alaba #8 of Austria arrives at the stadium before the FIFA World Cup 2026 Round of 32 match between Spain and Austria at Los Angeles Stadium on July 02, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Florencia Tan Jun/Getty Images)

"David [Alaba]'s arrival demonstrates the strength and ambition of the club, which does not want to rest on last season's positive results but is aiming for even greater things.

"David needs no introduction: he is a true champion who has played for clubs such as Real Madrid and Bayern Munich, and he will undoubtedly bring us invaluable experience and a winning mentality. We are delighted to have him," Zaniolo continued.

"He arrived with the utmost humility, which is ultimately what distinguishes a true champion from a player who is merely very good. I can only speak highly of him. He is one of the players we needed, and I cannot wait to play alongside him."

Zaniolo is currently injured so he'll miss the game against Udinese. He wasn't in good shape when Italy coach Roberto Mancini called him up during the latest international break, but Zaniolo was forced to pull out after the first match against Belgium, in which he didn't feature.

MILAN, ITALY – APRIL 11: Nicolo Zaniolo of Udinese Calcio is put under pressure by Davide Bartesaghi of AC Milan during the Serie A match between AC Milan and Udinese Calcio at Giuseppe Meazza Stadium on April 11, 2026 in Milan, Italy. (Photo by Marco Luzzani/Getty Images)

Zaniolo extended his contract with Udinese last summer after the Bianconeri had made his move from Galatasaray permanent, but negotiations were not straightforward.

"It was a somewhat turbulent summer, which made me reflect and understand what I really wanted," Zaniolo admitted.

"My intention was always to stay here because I have felt truly at home. Udinese is like a family to me: the club welcomed me, supported me and helped me in every way. I feel a strong sense of belonging and gratitude towards the club.

"There are many contractual dynamics in football… There were some negotiations, but fortunately everything worked out for the best," he added.

TURIN, ITALY – JANUARY 07: Nicolo Zaniolo of Udinese Calcio runs with the ball whilst under pressure from Guillermo Maripan of Torino during the Serie A match between Torino FC and Udinese Calcio at Stadio Olimpico di Torino on January 07, 2026 in Turin, Italy. (Photo by Valerio Pennicino/Getty Images)

The Italian striker confirmed he had attracted interest from other clubs before signing a new deal with the Bianconeri.

"When you have a good season, it is normal for there to be rumours linking you with big clubs, but I wanted to speak to Udinese first," he concluded.

"They wanted to keep me, and now it is up to me to repay their faith on the pitch."
